extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification and amendments satisfy the 35 U.S.C. 112 written description and enablement requirements and whether proposed amendments introduce new matter. Aimed at examination of claim support, priority/benefit dates, and proper treatment of amendments and replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An objective standard: 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed.' To satisfy the written description requirement an applicant must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention, and that the invention, in that context, is whatever is now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Vas-Cath, In re Gosteli, and related cases. The fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing Possession of the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession is shown by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means such as words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings, structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. See Lockwood, Pfaff, Regents v. Eli Lilly, Amgen v. Chugai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonliteral Description Permitted but Amendments Must Be Supported
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally (in haec verba) to satisfy the description requirement; however, if a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed (a departure, addition, or deletion) the claimed subject matter is not described in that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such amendments will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (written description) or denial of the benefit of an earlier filing date. See MPEP § 2163.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical Circumstances Raising Written Description Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues commonly arise when: (I) claims are amended or new claims are added; (II) reliance on the filing date of a parent application (35 U.S.C. 120); (III) reliance on foreign/provisional priority (35 U.S.C. 119); and (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often the issue arises upon claim amendments; an original claim rejection for lack of written description should be rare because of the strong presumption that the originally filed specification is adequate (see In re Wertheim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the Examiner and Presumption of Adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary is presented by the examiner; the examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and bears the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Marzocchi and In re Wertheim. The examiner must set forth express factual findings supporting a lack of written description conclusion (see MPEP § 2163).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Rejection Requirements (Identify Limitations and Prima Facie Case)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting for lack of written description the examiner must (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the filing time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention in view of the application disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general allegation such as 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. In some cases a simple statement pointing out lack of apparent support may be sufficient for new or amended claims where applicant has not pointed out support. See MPEP § 2163.04(I)(A)-(B) and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Treatment of Applicant Reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must review the basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 rejection in view of the record as a whole (amendments, arguments, and evidence). If the record demonstrates the written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection; if not, repeat and fully respond and properly treat any new showings (e.g., affidavits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When maintaining a rejection, thoroughly analyze and discuss any affidavits relevant to written description. See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement That Each Claim Limitation Be Supported
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to broadenings or narrowings, numerical ranges, and use of different terminology. See MPEP § 2163 and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening Claims — Omission of an Essential Limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise written description issues regarding whether the inventor possessed a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples include Gentry Gallery and Tronzo. If the specification makes clear that a particular narrow understanding is essential, removing that limitation can invalidate broader claims. Consider whether the original disclosure describes a feature as 'the only possible location' or 'outside the stated purpose' as indicating essentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a Generic Claim (Genus/Species Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written description for a claimed genus may be satisfied by describing a representative number of species that reflect variation within the genus; a single species may suffice only when the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus or when one skilled in the art would understand the disclosure to encompass the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If substantial variation exists within the genus, more species must be described. Cases: Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, In re Rasmussen, In re Herschler, In re Smythe. If ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species, one species is insufficient (In re Curtis, PTFE dental floss example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or Subgeneric Claim Changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing narrowing changes (subgeneric terminology or specific species) not supported by the as-filed disclosure can violate the written description requirement; a 'laundry list' disclosure of many possible moieties does not necessarily describe every species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case decided on its facts; examples include Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Ex parte Ohshiro. A subgenus may or may not be acceptable depending on whether species within it were disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range Limitations Must Be Supported
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical range limitations, the analysis must account for which ranges would be inherently supported by the original disclosure; claims that read literally on embodiments outside disclosed ranges may fail the description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: original '25%-60%' with examples '36%' and '50%' — a new limitation 'at least 35%' failed because it had no upper limit, whereas 'between 35% and 60%' met the requirement (In re Wertheim). Consider whether a skilled artisan would consider the broader range inherently supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of Written Description Requirement to New Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding content to the abstract, specification, or drawings that is not described in the application as filed raises a new matter issue; information from any one part of the application as filed may be added to any other part without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two statutory provisions prohibit new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no new matter in amendment) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue). See MPEP § 2163.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of New Matter — Examiner Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added, the examiner should object to the introduction of new matter under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 as appropriate and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to claims, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are unaffected per se but the specification is amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1 should be made. Applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments. Rejections are reviewable by the Board; objections to delete new matter are subject to petition (37 CFR 1.181). If both claims and specification contain new matter with both rejection and objection, the issue is appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Filed But Not Disclosed Elsewhere in Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If originally filed claims disclose material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter (providing proper antecedent basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form Paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and In re Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments Supported in Original Description Are Not New Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments that are supported in the original description are not new matter. Mere rephrasing that preserves the same meaning is permissible; inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing time would not be new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple definitions exist and a definition is added, it must be clear from the application as filed that applicant intended that definition to avoid new matter issues. Example: substituting a later-adopted technical name ('IFN-(a)') for an earlier generic term ('leukocyte interferon') may merely rename the invention and not introduce new matter (Scarring Corp. v. Megan). See In re Anderson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of Obvious Errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and its appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Odd. Special rules: a foreign priority document of record cannot be relied on to support correction of an error in the U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. For inadvertent omission of portions of the specification/drawings in U.S. applications filed on/after Sept 21, 2004, see 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.57(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent Function, Theory, or Advantage May Be Later Claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent application discloses a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, operates according to a theory, or has an advantage, the application necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if nothing explicit is said; the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities. See In re Reynolds, In re Smythe, In re Robertson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may incorporate content of another document by reference; the information incorporated becomes part of the application as filed and replacing the identified material with the actual text is not new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p). Incorporation by reference affects determinations under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, and 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph issues; see MPEP § 2181 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention defined by the claims; the disclosure must be sufficient to inform those skilled in the relevant art how to both make and use the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose is to communicate the invention to the public in a meaningful way. It is not necessary to enable a perfected, commercially viable embodiment unless so claimed. Enablement is separate and distinct from written description and must be analyzed on its own criteria. A claim is invalid if not supported by an enabling disclosure. See CFMT, Mineral Separation v. Hyde, and MPEP § 2164.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Enablement — Undue Experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The enablement inquiry asks whether the amount of experimentation required to practice the invention would be undue or unreasonable (the Mineral Separation undue experimentation standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the disclosure, when filed, contained sufficient information that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Consider the nature of the invention, state of the art, availability of routine optimization, quantity of guidance provided, and predictability of the art.
